hist_hint: 1985 to now, for the nearest state or region
hist_note: Modelled data, not station observations and not an official warning. Check figures against DMH records.
hist_err: History data is not available yet
hist_far: Figures describe the centre of {place}, {km} km away, so they are regional and less exact for your spot.
hist_cap_temp: Vertical = temperature (°C), horizontal = year. Each point is that year's 12-month mean. The dashed line is the 1991–2020 mean ({v}°C).
hist_cap_month: Vertical = rain that falls in the month (mm), horizontal = month. 30-year average, 1991–2020. The darker bar is this month.
hist_cap_enso: Each bar = total Jun–Sep rain (mm), averaged over the years with that ENSO phase.
hist_agri_line: In {place}, Jun–Sep rain in {n} El Niño years was {pct}% {dir} than in neutral years ({a} mm vs {b} mm).
hist_agri_warn: Few years and modelled data, so this is only a guide. Check the DMH seasonal outlook before choosing planting dates.
cmp_read: How to read: the green part is the normal range, the dot is today, the vertical line is the average or median. Compared with ERA5 1991–2020.
cmp_t_band: Normal range = middle 80% of past years (lowest and highest 10% left out)
cmp_r_band: Normal range = middle third of past years
cmp_wb: Compare the two bars. More rain than evaporation means the ground is getting wetter; less means it is drying.
help_feels_b: Temperature, humidity and wind combined. Humid air feels hotter than the thermometer says, and wind feels cooler. Use this number for how your body will cope.
help_humid_b: How much water vapour is in the air. Near 100% sweat cannot evaporate, so heat feels worse, and early mornings can turn misty.
help_uv_b: How strongly sunlight can harm skin. 0–2 low, 3–5 moderate, 6–7 high, 8–10 very high, 11+ extreme (WHO scale). From 3 up, use sunglasses, a hat and sunscreen, and seek shade between 10:00 and 16:00.
help_aqi_b: US AQI scale: 0–50 good, 51–100 moderate, 101–150 unhealthy for sensitive groups, 151–200 unhealthy, 201–300 very unhealthy, 300+ hazardous. PM2.5 is fine dust that can reach the lungs. Above 100, children, older people and people with breathing problems should limit time outdoors.
help_wind_b: Wind speed is the average. A gust is a brief peak that can be far stronger, so for boats, roofing and loose items look at the gust figure.
help_chance_b: The chance, not the amount. 100% means the forecasts agree on at least a trace (0.1 mm) somewhere in the area, not a promise for your street. The daily figure is the highest single hour. About 3 in 10 days marked 70% staying dry is normal.
help_amount_b: Daily total. Under 2.5 mm drizzle, 2.5–15 light, 16–64 moderate, 65–115 heavy, 116–204 very heavy, 205+ extreme (IMD classes). Chance and amount are separate: a high chance with under 1 mm may pass unnoticed.
help_area_b: One forecast speaks for roughly a 10–25 km area. Showers are only a few km wide, so they can fall next door and miss you. A small shift in wind direction can move the rain track.
help_far_b: Accuracy drops with distance. Days 1–3 are dependable and 4–7 are a rough guide. Check again daily, because it changes.
help_icon_b: One picture stands for the whole day, so a rain icon can appear for just a few wet hours. For timing, use the hourly strip on the Today tab.
help_era5_b: The weather around the same date in the last 30 years. Data is ERA5 (ECMWF/Copernicus), a blend of observations and a computer model, not an exact reading from one station.
help_band_b: For temperature: the middle 80% of 30 years, with the coldest and hottest 10% left out. For rain: the middle third when 30 years are split into low, middle and high. A dot outside the green means unusual, not necessarily dangerous.
help_anom_b: The difference is how much hotter or cooler than normal. A percentile of 90 means hotter than 90% of the last 30 years on similar dates.
help_trend_b: A straight line through yearly average temperatures, giving the rise over 10 years. Year-to-year swings mean the number carries uncertainty. Data from 1985 is modelled.
help_enso_b: Warm or cool swings in the Pacific. In El Niño years monsoon rain tends to be lower in some parts of Myanmar, but it varies by region (almost no difference in some). A tendency, not a verdict on any season.
help_water_b: Compares rain that fell with water lost to evaporation (ET). More rain means the ground wets up, more evaporation means it dries. A rough guide for farming only.
help_soil_b: How much water each cubic metre of soil holds. Higher is wetter, but it depends on soil type, so compare with a week ago rather than judging one number.
help_notofficial_b: This page shows data and calculations. For floods, cyclones and earthquakes follow the Department of Meteorology and Hydrology (DMH).
hist_cap_ci: A range instead of one number shows honest uncertainty; the narrower it is, the steadier the data.
hist_sig: The difference is significant (more than chance, p {p})
hist_nosig: The difference is too small to tell from chance (p {p})
hist_agri_nosig: In {place} the Jun–Sep rain gap between El Niño and neutral years ({pct}%) is not significant. Do not assume El Niño means less rain here.
hist_p_note: p is the chance of seeing a gap this large by luck. Below 0.05 is treated as significant.
fa_note: Computed from the forecast, not official warnings. Looks at the next 3 days.
global_note: This place is outside Myanmar, so only the basics are shown: weather, forecast, Compare, and storm/quake feeds. For local official warnings, check that country's weather service.
watch_note: News published by DMH — keep an eye on it. This is not an official DMH warning; open the DMH page yourself.
cmp_m2: Today's values are forecasts or recent model data, not station measurements. One grid cell is about 30 km wide, so your exact spot can differ.
cmp_m3: The normal range does not mean "good" or "bad"; it only shows how far a value is from normal.
enso_strong_label: Strong to very strong through Jan–Mar 2027

cmp_visible_caveat: Note: This compares weather-model estimates with the 1991–2020 ERA5 historical reference. It is not a station observation or an official warning; a difference from normal does not automatically mean hazardous conditions.
agrx_fert_caution_body: Distinguish verified source-backed guidance from general references below. The N:P:K ratios are not a prescription for your field. Test your soil and follow advice from your local agriculture office.
help_temp_t: Why does my phone show a different temperature?
help_temp_b: This app shows the temperature calculated by the ECMWF model for a grid cell about 9 km wide. It is not a measurement. Phone apps may use another source or the nearest station, so 1–3 degrees of difference is normal, and two nearby towns in the same cell can look alike. To compare, check the data time shown above (date and hour); a different hour gives a different number.

hist_scope: This section is not for a single town. It shows modelled data for a whole state/region since 1985. The “today vs normal” comparison above is for your selected place.
hist_cap_rain_year: Each bar is one year of rain. Colour shows that year's ENSO phase; the dashed line is the 1991–2020 average.
mc_intro: How much each month of {y} differs from the {a}–{b} normal, for average temperature and total rain. Above the line = warmer or wetter than normal; below = cooler or drier.
mc_through: ERA5 data is only available up to {d} (it runs a few days behind).
mc_partial: {m}: month not over — only {n} days so far. The normal is also taken for the same {n} days.
mc_source: Source: both this year and the normal ({a}–{b}) come from the ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF/Copernicus) via Open-Meteo. It is modelled data, not a weather-station record.
mc_err: Month-by-month comparison is not available right now.
mc_unavail: No month-by-month comparison data for this place yet.
mc_aria_temp: Chart of each month's average temperature against normal
mc_aria_rain: Chart of each month's rain total against normal
fg_moon_tide_now: Near a full or new moon, so tides can run higher. Coasts, river mouths and tidal rivers are more likely to flood.
fg_moon_tide_note: Tides run higher around full and new moon. People on the coast, at river mouths and on tidal rivers should take care.
fg_moon_approx: Calculated with the Myanmar calendar rules. It can differ by a day from a printed calendar.
fg_hyd_work: When working in the heat, drink 1 cup (about 240 ml) of water every 15–20 minutes, before you feel thirsty. Frequent small drinks work better than a lot at once.
fg_hyd_cap: Do not drink more than 1.4 litres an hour. Too much water can also be dangerous because it lowers blood salt.
fg_hyd_salt: Eat regular meals; food supplies the salt you lose. Do not take salt tablets. If you sweat for several hours, a drink with balanced electrolytes is fine.
fg_hyd_rest: On very hot days, allow more rest and water breaks. If you are not used to the heat, work shorter hours for the first days.
fg_sos_sub: Once opened, it can be read without an internet connection.
fg_sos_light_1: As soon as you hear thunder, go into a sturdy building or a car. Nowhere outside is safe.
fg_sos_light_2: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder. If you hear thunder again in that time, restart the 30 minutes.
fg_sos_light_3: Stay away from open fields, trees, metal and water. Indoors, do not touch plumbing or phone lines, and unplug electrical devices.
fg_sos_light_4: Someone struck by lightning is safe to touch; they carry no charge. Call emergency services at once.
fg_sos_quake_1: Drop to your hands and knees, cover your head and neck under a sturdy table or with your arms, and hold on until the shaking stops.
fg_sos_quake_2: If you are inside, stay inside; do not run outside. Keep away from windows and outside walls. In bed, stay there and cover your head with a pillow.
fg_sos_quake_3: If you are outside, stay outside and move away from buildings, power lines and trees.
fg_sos_quake_4: Near the coast, if shaking lasts more than 20 seconds or when it stops, a tsunami may follow: go at once to ground 3 km from the shore or 30 m above sea level.
fg_sos_flood_1: Do not walk through moving water. Fast water 15 cm (6 in) deep can knock you down, and 30 cm (1 ft) can carry a car away.
fg_sos_flood_2: Do not drive through flooded roads; turn around. You cannot tell how deep the water is.
fg_sos_flood_3: If authorities tell you to leave, go to higher ground at once. Keep away from fallen power lines and from water touching them.
fg_sos_heat_1: Confusion, slurred speech, fainting, seizures or a very high body temperature can mean heat stroke. Call emergency services immediately.
fg_sos_heat_2: Until help arrives, move to shade and cool the person at once. Cold-water immersion is best. Otherwise put cold wet towels or ice on the head, neck, body, armpits and groin, and fan them.
fg_sos_heat_3: Never leave the person alone. If they are awake and alert, let them sip cool water.
fg_sos_numbers: Emergency phone numbers are in the Emergency numbers card.

leaf_key_title: AI second look: your own key
leaf_key_intro: The AI second look is optional and runs on your own Anthropic API key, so the cost goes to your account, not to this app. Without a key everything else in the Lab still works.
leaf_key_how: How your key is handled: with each check it goes over HTTPS through this app's server to Anthropic. The server does not save it, log it or share it. On this phone it is kept until you close this tab; tick “Remember on this device” to keep it longer.
leaf_key_where: You can create a key in the Anthropic Console (API keys). Treat it like a password, and set a spending limit for it there.

leaf_key_err_format: That does not look like an Anthropic key. It starts with sk-ant- and has no spaces.

leaf_key_shared: On this server the AI look also works without a key (up to {n} per hour).

leaf_tips_title: How to take a good leaf photo
leaf_tip_1: Pick one leaf that shows the problem, ideally half healthy and half affected.
leaf_tip_2: Fill most of the frame with that leaf. Close enough to see the spots, not so close that it goes soft.
leaf_tip_3: Use daylight. Shade or a cloudy sky is best; avoid direct sun glare and the flash.
leaf_tip_4: Hold the phone steady and tap the leaf on the screen so it is in focus.
leaf_tip_5: Put a plain background behind the leaf (your hand, a sheet of paper). Wipe off dust and water drops first.
leaf_tip_6: Take a second photo of the whole plant and a third of the field edge, and note since when. Show all of them to your extension officer.
leaf_q_title: A quick look at the photo (on this phone only)
leaf_q_dark: This photo looks too dark. Move into daylight or shade and take it again.
leaf_q_bright: This photo looks washed out by strong light. Move into shade, avoid glare, and take it again.
leaf_q_far: Hardly any leaf colour in the middle of this photo. Move closer so one leaf fills most of the frame.
leaf_q_blurry: This photo may be blurry. Hold the phone steady, tap the leaf to focus, and take it again.
leaf_q_cap: Because of this, the photo reading is shown as “not sure”.
leaf_oc_title: Not every sign is a disease
leaf_oc_clue: A disease or an insect usually leaves something you can see on the plant (fungus, ooze, the insects) and spreads from plant to plant over days. Nutrient, water, heat and chemical problems do not spread from plant to plant and often hit many kinds of plants alike. A stressed plant can have both.
leaf_oc_nitrogen_d: Older, lower leaves turn pale yellow first and plants stay small and thin. The whole field or a whole patch looks the same.
leaf_oc_zinc_d: Lower leaves turn pale or rusty brown, often near the base of the leaf, and plants stay small. It shows in patches in the field.
leaf_oc_iron_d: Small brown spots on lower leaves start at the tips and move toward the base and the upper leaves. Common in wet, acid soils.
leaf_oc_potassium_d: Older leaves show uneven yellow and dead patches and look bluish-green. Straw is weak and plants fall over.
leaf_oc_water_d: In the hottest part of the day leaves roll, wilt or dry at the tips and edges, and recover after rain or watering. Many kinds of plants in the same place look alike.
leaf_oc_flood_d: Leaves turn yellow and wilt even though the soil is wet. Low spots in the field are worst.
leaf_oc_heat_d: Brown or bleached dry patches on leaf tips and on the side facing the sun, often after very hot days. It does not spread over the next days.
leaf_oc_chem_d: Leaves curl, twist or spot soon after a spray, or after a neighbour sprayed. Many kinds of plants are hit and it does not spread from plant to plant afterwards.
leaf_oc_dust_d: Marks or a white film that wipe off with a damp finger. Wipe one leaf before you decide.
leaf_oc_age_d: Only the oldest, lowest leaves turn yellow and dry while the newer leaves stay green.
leaf_help: Ask your nearest agriculture extension office if the signs spread over a few days, if more than a few plants are affected, if you are not sure, and before you use any chemical. Take 3 photos (whole plant, a close leaf, the affected part) and note since when and what the weather has been.
leaf_hs_intro: General advice from WHO, FAO and CDC. It is not a diagnosis and does not replace a doctor or health worker. In an emergency go to the nearest health facility (the Hospitals tab can help you find one).
leaf_hs_spray_1: Read the label and follow it. Never use more or less than it says.
leaf_hs_spray_2: Wear gloves, a face mask and long clothes when you mix or spray.
leaf_hs_spray_3: Do not eat, drink or smoke while you work with chemicals. Never blow or suck on a blocked nozzle.
leaf_hs_spray_4: Wash well with soap afterwards, and wash the skin at once if it was splashed.
leaf_hs_spray_5: Keep chemicals locked away from children, animals and food, in their own labelled containers.
leaf_hs_spray_6: Never reuse an empty container for food or water.
leaf_hs_spray_7: If you feel sick or dizzy, get a rash or vomit, stop work and get medical help right away. Take the label with you.
leaf_hs_heat_1: Drink water regularly: about a cup every hour and at least 2–3 litres a day.
leaf_hs_heat_2: Rest in the shade, avoid heavy work in the hottest hours, and wear light, loose clothes.
leaf_hs_heat_3: Wet your skin or clothes with water to cool down.
leaf_hs_heat_4: Confusion, fainting or very hot skin can mean heatstroke, which is an emergency. Move the person to shade, cool them down and get medical help at once.
leaf_hs_water_1: After rain, empty or cover containers that hold water. Clean and cover stored water every week.
leaf_hs_water_2: Dengue mosquitoes bite in the daytime. Wear long clothes, use repellent (DEET, picaridin or IR3535) and sleep under a net.
leaf_hs_water_3: Warning signs of severe dengue often appear after the fever goes down: severe belly pain, constant vomiting, fast breathing, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, cold pale skin, extreme weakness or restlessness. Get care immediately.
leaf_hs_water_4: Avoid wading in floodwater. Wear waterproof boots and cover cuts with a waterproof dressing.
leaf_hs_water_5: Fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, red eyes or yellow skin within 2–30 days of contact with floodwater or wet soil: see a health worker and tell them where you worked.
leaf_hs_water_6: After floods drink only boiled or treated water and wash hands with soap. For diarrhoea use oral rehydration solution (ORS). See a health worker for blood in the stool, sunken eyes, poor drinking, or diarrhoea lasting 14 days or more.
leaf_hs_snake_1: Keep the person calm and completely still, and splint the bitten limb. Take off rings, bracelets and anklets near the bite.
leaf_hs_snake_2: Get to a health facility as fast as you can.
leaf_hs_snake_3: Do not cut the wound, suck it, tie a tight band around the limb, or use herbal remedies.
leaf_hs_snake_4: On the way, tell the doctor about any bleeding, drooping eyelids or trouble breathing.
leaf_hs_snake_5: Wear boots and long trousers in tall grass and flooded fields.
wx_mosquito_text: Empty or cover containers that hold water. Dengue mosquitoes bite in the daytime, so wear long sleeves and use repellent.
wx_floodwater_text: Stay out of floodwater and cover cuts. Drink only boiled or treated water and wash hands with soap.
